title: How Do You Evaluate a Transistor Replacement When the Original Part Is No Longer Available?
gist: A practitioner checklist for qualifying a substitute transistor when the original goes obsolete, arguing that parametric-search equivalence is misleading: switching characteristics, package and pinout, thermal behavior, datasheet test conditions and lifecycle status all decide whether a 'matching' part actually works in-circuit. The piece ends as an open question to engineers about which parameters they treat as mandatory before approving a replacement.

insights.claim: A transistor that looks similar on a parametric search can still behave differently in the actual circuit, because the replacement must work under the same electrical, thermal and mechanical conditions as the original.
insights.speaker: SemiWiki
insights.so_what: Distributor cross-reference tools understate requalification cost, a hidden expense in obsolescence-driven redesigns.
insights.quote: A device that looks similar on a parametric search may still behave differently in the actual circuit.

insights.claim: A replacement device should provide margin against actual operating conditions rather than merely matching the original part's nominal voltage and current ratings.
insights.speaker: SemiWiki
insights.so_what: Design-margin discipline, not spec matching, determines field failure rates on long-life hardware.
insights.locator: However, the replacement should provide sufficient margin

insights.claim: A commonly overlooked failure mode is that RDS(on), current rating and power dissipation may be specified at different gate voltages or temperatures across datasheets, so raw numbers are not comparable without their test conditions.
insights.speaker: SemiWiki
insights.so_what: Any automated or AI-driven parts-substitution tool that ignores test conditions will generate silently wrong recommendations.
insights.quote: engineers should compare not only the numbers, but also the conditions under which those numbers were measured

themes.theme: Parameters that decide switching and thermal behavior

insights.claim: Two MOSFETs with similar RDS(on) can have very different gate charge, and in a high-frequency converter that difference can change switching losses considerably.
insights.speaker: SemiWiki
insights.so_what: Efficiency claims in power-supply designs hinge on gate charge as much as conduction resistance; a like-for-like swap can silently cut converter efficiency.
insights.quote: two MOSFETs may have similar RDS(on) but very different gate charges

insights.claim: Gate charge, switching speed, capacitance, rise/fall time and reverse-recovery behavior affect efficiency, EMI and thermal performance, so switching parameters can dominate over headline voltage and current ratings in switching applications.
insights.speaker: SemiWiki
insights.so_what: EMI re-certification is a downstream cost of any switching-parameter mismatch, adding schedule risk to obsolescence swaps.
insights.locator: For switching applications, parameters beyond voltage

insights.claim: Power dissipation depends on the transistor plus PCB layout, cooling conditions, operating temperature and actual circuit losses, so an electrically equivalent replacement may still run at a different temperature in the same design.
insights.speaker: SemiWiki
insights.so_what: Thermal re-verification on the real board is non-optional; bench-equivalent parts can shorten product life in the field.

insights.claim: A device with similar electrical specifications may still force PCB modifications if package type, pin configuration, pin spacing, thermal pad or footprint differ, converting a parts swap into a board respin.
insights.speaker: SemiWiki
insights.so_what: Package mismatch is where obsolescence costs escalate from procurement to engineering NRE and requalification.
insights.quote: A device with similar electrical specifications may still require PCB modifications if the pinout or package is different.

insights.claim: Replacing a hard-to-source transistor with another device that has limited availability simply recreates the same shortage problem, so lifecycle status and supply stability can matter as much as electrical specifications for long-life products.
insights.speaker: SemiWiki
insights.so_what: Discrete-semiconductor suppliers with credible long-term-supply commitments can command a premium in industrial, aerospace and defense sockets.
insights.quote: replacing it with another device that has limited availability may simply create the same problem again

insights.claim: Approval priorities differ by device class: power MOSFET swaps hinge on VDS, RDS(on), gate charge and thermal performance, BJT swaps on gain and saturation characteristics, and RF applications add a further set of requirements.
insights.speaker: SemiWiki
insights.so_what: No single substitution rule scales across a BOM, which limits how far automated sourcing tools can reduce engineering labor.
